claim: The global diabetes prevalence in 20–79 year-old was estimated to be 10.5% (536.6 million people) in 2021.
source: According to the latest epidemiological data from the International Diabetes Federation, the global diabetes prevalence in 20–79 year-old was estimated to be 10.5% (536.6 million people) in 2021, and is expected to rise to 12.2% (783.2 million) in 2045 (Sun et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2022 reporting epidemiological data from the International Diabetes Federation.

claim: The global diabetes prevalence is expected to rise to 12.2% (783.2 million) in 2045.
source: According to the latest epidemiological data from the International Diabetes Federation, the global diabetes prevalence in 20–79 year-old was estimated to be 10.5% (536.6 million people) in 2021, and is expected to rise to 12.2% (783.2 million) in 2045 (Sun et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2022 reporting projected epidemiological data.

claim: Type 2 diabetes is associated with irreversible risk factors such as age, genetics, race, and ethnicity.
source: With the development of genomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, it has been discovered by many studies that type 2 diabetes is associated with irreversible risk factors such as age, genetics, race, and ethnicity and reversible factors such as diet, physical activity, and lifestyle (Heald et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Heald et al., 2020 and Chan et al., 2021 describing risk factors for type 2 diabetes.

claim: Type 2 diabetes is associated with reversible factors such as diet, physical activity, and lifestyle.
source: With the development of genomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, it has been discovered by many studies that type 2 diabetes is associated with irreversible risk factors such as age, genetics, race, and ethnicity and reversible factors such as diet, physical activity, and lifestyle (Heald et al., 2020; Chan et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Heald et al., 2020 and Chan et al., 2021 describing risk factors for type 2 diabetes.

claim: Aerobic metabolism in glucose oxidation, mitochondrial damage, and oxidative stress play a critical role in the occurrence and development of diabetes.
source: Aerobic metabolism in glucose oxidation, mitochondrial damage, and oxidative stress have been considered to play a critical role in the occurrence and development of diabetes (Iacobini et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Iacobini et al., 2021 discussing the role of oxidative stress in diabetes.

claim: Exercise and antioxidant supplements are often suggested as essential therapeutic strategies in the early stages of type 2 diabetes.
source: Exercise and antioxidant supplements are often suggested as essential therapeutic strategies in the early stages of type 2 diabetes (Kirwan et al., 2017; Bhatti et al., 2022), with different mechanisms.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kirwan et al., 2017 and Bhatti et al., 2022 discussing therapeutic strategies for type 2 diabetes.

claim: Chronic exercise training can alleviate oxidative stress and diabetic symptoms by improving cellular mitochondrial function and biogenesis in the diabetic state.
source: It has been reported that chronic exercise training can alleviate oxidative stress and diabetic symptoms by improving cellular mitochondrial function and biogenesis in the diabetic state (Stanford and Goodyear, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stanford and Goodyear, 2014 reporting effects of chronic exercise training.

claim: Exercise increases reactive oxygen species (ROS) production.
source: Contradictorily, exercise also increases reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, while prolonged or high-intensity exercise could result in mitochondrial functional impairment to aggravate complications of diabetes (Flockhart et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Flockhart et al., 2021 discussing ROS production during exercise.

claim: Prolonged or high-intensity exercise could result in mitochondrial functional impairment to aggravate complications of diabetes.
source: Contradictorily, exercise also increases reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, while prolonged or high-intensity exercise could result in mitochondrial functional impairment to aggravate complications of diabetes (Flockhart et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Flockhart et al., 2021 discussing effects of high-intensity exercise.

claim: 1 hr of moderate endurance exercise can increase lipid peroxidation in humans.
source: Since 1970s, studies have demonstrated that 1 hr of moderate endurance exercise can increase lipid peroxidation in humans (Brady et al., 1979; Dillard et al., 1978).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brady et al., 1979 and Dillard et al., 1978 demonstrating lipid peroxidation during exercise.

claim: Ashton directly detected increasing free radical levels in exercising humans using electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy (EPR) and spin capture in 1998.
source: In 1998, Ashton directly detected increasing free radical levels in exercising humans using electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy (EPR) and spin capture (Ashton et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ashton et al., 1998 describing direct detection of free radicals during exercise.

claim: James D Watson hypothesized that type 2 diabetes is accelerated by insufficient oxidative stress rather than oxidative stress.
source: Regarding the contradiction of exercise on ROS scavenging or production, James D Watson also hypothesized that type 2 diabetes is accelerated by insufficient oxidative stress rather than oxidative stress (Watson, 2014), based on the effect of exercise on diabetes management.
evidence: Supported by citation to Watson, 2014 presenting a hypothesis about oxidative stress and diabetes.

claim: Antioxidants reduce cytotoxic ROS and oxidative products, thus alleviating diabetes and achieving glycemic control.
source: In contrast, the general view of the antioxidant treatment for diabetes is that antioxidants reduce cytotoxic ROS and oxidative products, thus alleviating diabetes and achieving glycemic control (Rahimi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rahimi et al., 2005 describing the mechanism of antioxidant treatment for diabetes.

claim: Hepatic mitochondrial ROS scavengers and antioxidant substances inhibited the oxidative products such as Malondialdehyde (MDA) and 4-HNE in diabetic animals and favored glycemic control.

claim: The increase of skeletal muscle glucose uptake during exercise is crucial in glycemic control.

claim: The activation of hepatic AMPK alleviates diabetes symptoms by reducing glycogen synthesis, increasing glycolysis, and promoting glucose absorption in surrounding tissues.

claim: AMPK could be activated by hydrogen peroxide stimulation through direct oxidative modification.

claim: Under a low ROS microenvironment, GRXs mediated S-glutathione modification activates AMPK to improve glucose utilization.

claim: Endogenous antioxidant defences increase to counteract increased levels of ROS induced by exercise.

claim: Different levels of ROS generated by exercise have differential regulations on the activity and expression of hepatic AMPK.
source: During exercise, different levels of ROS generated by exercise have differential regulations on the activity and expression of hepatic AMPK.
evidence: Stated as a finding from the current study.

claim: Moderate exercise-derived ROS promoted hepatic AMPK glutathionylation activation.
source: Moderate exercise-derived ROS promoted hepatic AMPK glutathionylation activation.
